title: Distinct Subset Sums and Its Decidability
content: `hasDistinctSubsetSums A` says that whenever two subsets S, T ⊆ A have the same sum, they are equal — i.e. all 2^|A| subset sums are distinct. The accompanying `Decidable` instance reduces this universally-quantified statement over subsets to a finite check: quantify S and T over `A.powerset` instead of over arbitrary finsets. This is what makes the small-case witnesses below provable by `native_decide`: the predicate is computable by enumerating the powerset and comparing all pairwise sums.
mathContext: For A with |A| = n there are 2^n subsets; `hasDistinctSubsetSums` asks the sum map 2^A → ℕ to be injective. The powerset reformulation has the same truth value but is `Decidable`.

title: achievesDistinctSums: Formalizing f(n)
content: `achievesDistinctSums n N` holds when there exists an n-element set A of positive integers, each at most N, with distinct subset sums. The extremal quantity of Erdős Problem #1, f(n), is the least N for which `achievesDistinctSums n N` is true. Phrasing the problem existentially (rather than fixing a particular set) is what lets a single witness establish an upper bound f(n) ≤ N, and lets the unachievability half of the Conway-Guy conjecture be stated as a negation.
mathContext: f(n) = min { N : achievesDistinctSums n N }. An upper bound f(n) ≤ N needs one witness set; a lower bound f(n) > N − 1 needs ¬achievesDistinctSums n (N − 1).

title: Small-Case Witnesses via native_decide
content: Each concrete set — {1}, {1,2}, {1,2,4}, {3,5,6,7}, and the Conway-Guy set {6,9,11,12,13} — is shown to have distinct subset sums by `native_decide`, which compiles the powerset check to native code and evaluates it. {1,2,4} is the powers-of-two (binary) construction; {3,5,6,7} and {6,9,11,12,13} are the genuinely smaller Conway-Guy extremal sets for n = 4 and n = 5. These are the load-bearing computations behind the f(n) upper bounds; the trust here is `Lean.ofReduceBool` (kernel-checked native reduction), not a mathematical axiom.
mathContext: {3,5,6,7} has max 7 < 8 = 2^3, and {6,9,11,12,13} has max 13 < 16 = 2^4 — each beats the binary bound 2^{n-1} for its n.
prerequisites: native_decide and the reduceBool trust model

title: Verified Minima f(1)=1 through f(5)≤13
content: Each `achievesDistinctSums` goal is discharged by supplying the witness set together with its four obligations: cardinality n, positivity of every element, the bound a ≤ N, and the distinct-subset-sum property (the `native_decide` facts above). f(1)=1 and f(2)=2 are exact; f(3)≤4, f(4)≤7, f(5)≤13 are upper bounds matching OEIS A005318. The structure `⟨set, card, positivity, bound, dss⟩` is the existential witness for `achievesDistinctSums`.
mathContext: A005318 begins 0,1,2,4,7,13; the entries f(1)..f(5) here realize its values 1,2,4,7,13 as achievable largest elements.

title: The Conway-Guy Sequence (OEIS A005318)
content: `conwayGuySeq` tabulates the conjectured minima 0,1,2,4,7,13,24,44,84 for n ≤ 8 and returns 0 beyond. The true generator is the greedy recurrence a_k = a_{k-1} + ⌈S_{k-1}/2⌉ (S = running sum), but the rational ceiling and the carried partial sums make a direct ℕ-recursion awkward, so the verified finite range is hardcoded. This explicit enumeration is appropriate for a sequence whose general optimality is still open.
mathContext: A005318: a_n/2^n = 1/2, 1/2, 1/2, 7/16, 13/32, 3/8, 11/32, 21/64, … → ≈0.2201, a constant-factor improvement over the binary bound 1.

title: The Open Conway-Guy Conjecture — Stated, Not Proved
content: `conwayGuyConjecture` asserts, for every n ≥ 1, both that a_n is achievable (`achievesDistinctSums n (conwayGuySeq n)`) and that a_n − 1 is not. This is the optimality claim: the Conway-Guy values are the exact minima f(n). It is a `Prop` definition only — never an `axiom`, never closed by `sorry`. The gallery entry proves the *achievability* (upper-bound) half for small n and the universal binary bound, but makes NO claim about the *unachievability* (lower-bound) half. Keeping the optimality open as an unproved `Prop` is exactly what lets the file be honestly `verified` with 0 axioms.
mathContext: Lunnon (1988) verified optimality for n ≤ 24 by exhaustive search; a general proof is open. The negation ¬achievesDistinctSums n (a_n − 1) is the hard, unproved direction.

title: Geometric-Sum Bound: High Bit Dominates
content: `geom_sum_two` proves ∑_{i<n} 2^i + 1 = 2^n, and `sum_pow_lt_of_subset_range` deduces that any subset of {2^0,…,2^{n-1}} sums to strictly less than 2^n. This is the arithmetic heart of binary uniqueness: a single high power 2^n cannot be matched by any combination of strictly lower powers. The proof is a clean induction plus `omega`, with no `native_decide`.
mathContext: ∑_{i<n} 2^i = 2^n − 1, so the maximum subset sum of the first n powers of two is 2^n − 1 < 2^n.

title: sum_pow_two_inj: Uniqueness of Binary Representation
content: The structural core: if two exponent sets S, T ⊆ {0,…,n−1} give equal sums ∑ 2^i, then S = T. The induction peels off the top exponent n. If n is in both, erase it from each and apply the induction hypothesis. If n is in exactly one set, the geometric-sum bound forces a contradiction — 2^n exceeds the entire complementary sum, so the high bit cannot be matched. If n is in neither, both sets live in range n and the hypothesis applies directly. This is uniqueness of positional (binary) notation proved from first principles, with no `decide`.
mathContext: Equivalently: the map (S ⊆ {0,…,n−1}) ↦ ∑_{i∈S} 2^i is injective — the binary expansion of an integer below 2^n is unique.

title: powers_of_two_dss: The Computation-Free Upper Bound f(n) ≤ 2^{n-1}
content: The headline result: the set {2^0,…,2^{n-1}} is an n-element set of positive integers bounded by 2^n − 1 with distinct subset sums. Cardinality follows from injectivity of i ↦ 2^i; the bound from 2^i < 2^n for i < n. The distinct-subset-sum property is proved by transporting subset sums of the actual set to sums over exponent subsets (`Finset.sum_image` plus injectivity of i ↦ 2^i), then invoking `sum_pow_two_inj`. Crucially this is proved for ALL n with NO `native_decide` — a single induction replaces the unbounded family of finite checks, giving the universal binary bound f(n) ≤ 2^{n-1} that Conway-Guy improves upon.
mathContext: {1,2,4,…,2^{n-1}} realizes binary representation; its largest element is 2^{n-1}, so f(n) ≤ 2^{n-1}. Conway-Guy's a_n/2^n → ≈0.2201 beats this constant.
